policy_title: Impose 5-year residency and employment requirement for benefits
stated: Reform UK will require 5 years of residency and employment to claim any benefits in the UK, aiming to stop health tourism and immediate access to welfare.

source.quote: Stop Health Tourism and Immediate Access to Benefits We will impose a requirement of 5 years residency and employment to claim any benefits in the UK.

bearing_set.reason: Denying all benefits to those without 5 years' residency/employment directly removes income support, housing benefit, and tax credits from that population, materially reducing their ability to afford essentials.
The policy explicitly targets 'health tourism', suggesting restricted NHS/healthcare entitlement for those below the threshold, directly affecting healthcare access for that group.

Eliminating the safety net for any worker who loses their job before the 5-year threshold removes job security and weakens bargaining power, moving the in-work poverty and job security/quality indicators for that cohort.

A blanket denial of all benefits regardless of individual circumstances (acquired disability, involuntary redundancy, childcare needs) engages the equal treatment / anti-discrimination protections and due process indicators under O9's strict scope, and raises concrete ECHR Article 14 / Protocol 1 Article 1 questions.

Restricting benefit eligibility for any resident below the 5-year threshold reduces welfare expenditure, producing a material improvement in the public-spending/debt path — the primary fiscal mechanism the policy operates through.

Those excluded are disproportionately lower-income recent migrants; removing means-tested safety nets specifically from this group widens the income gap between the top and bottom, worsening inequality on a distributional basis.

membership_note: Four genuine bearings: an equal-treatment/due-process effect (O9), a job-security/labour-vulnerability effect (O4), a direct fiscal saving (O12), and an inequality-widening distributional effect (O14). O2 (cost of living for those affected) is a real channel but is adequately captured within the O14 inequality signal and does not add a distinct verdict. O3 is not in scope unless NHS access is explicitly restricted (standard UK practice treats NHS as separate from welfare benefits).
